I was clumsy in my wording of my initial point. And I apologise for that.

I don't feel like I have ownership over the code that AI has created to such a degree that I feel aggrieved that someone can decompile it and have that as something to work from.  
  
Having your game be copied from underneath you when you've invested a lot of time is a huge shame, don't get me wrong.  
  
Ultimately, at this point in my own game's development process, it's early enough that if someone were to decompile it and attempt to release it in some form, I wouldn't care. Because there's still a lot of creative direction and changes that I'm looking to make.

But then as I said, it's easy for me to say that whilst I'm at this point, compared to someone who has actually released something.

replies.author: taisui

Laundered code is still infringing code. In real litigation, civil discovery pulls your prompts, commit history, and scratchpads. An LLM acting as a code-scrambler doesn't magically turn a derivative work into an independent creation.

replies.author: superkickstart
replies.body:
It's a bit muddy situation right now but assets can be used and copied freely if they are purely ai generated. If a developer generates a rock texture and uses it unchanged, there may be no copyright in that texture. If an artist creatively repaints it, or incorporates their own drawing, those human-authored elements can be protected.

ideas and mechanics can't really be protected. Also, same basic human authorship rule applies to AI-generated code. Code does not get an exemption just because it is software.

By example, when Hasbro tried to sue Words with Friends for ripping off scrabble, right down to the board layout, the letter scores, and the rules, the courts said "get fucked."

Why?  Because words with friends switched the colors of the bonus squares, meaning there was no likelihood a customer would confuse the two games, and ***nothing else breached copyright***.

We've done this so many times.  Trivial Pursuit is rolling in its grave right now.  They copied the entire question and answer list from a book, and got away with it.

We need to define what 'cloning' means here. Does it mean giving the game to an AI and asking it to make a clone? Is the clone exact? Or are you just making a shitty knock-off? 

If your game is so similar to the original that people could confuse it with that, you are very much on the hook. Your "Big Vehicle Larceny" having cars you can steal, gunfights with police and missions is very much a case of copying someone else's game and just changing the names - everyone knows it's the Abibas version of GTA, and could thus hurt its sales.

If it's neither, then you're just making a knock-off and no one gives a shit.

It's a shame that games are being copied/cloned, but these games are just too simple and are too easily replicated. I find it disgusting when someone copies a game exactly using the same assets and everything and they should be held accountable if possible.

I think people have to realise that these simple games with basic shallow mechanics, and simple graphics are close to worthless in 2026. If you are expecting to sell a game on steam or something, the bar is much higher now. To create value in a game it requires depth, layered mechanics, lore, refinement, polished gameplay etc. Also if you don't want your graphic style to be copied you have to create quality aesthetics which takes time to replicate. 

This is the reality of game dev now, and unless you have some kind of copyright claim on an IP, trademark, imagery etc. Then complaining about it won't really change anything.

I have learnt to accept this and adapt, and people have to adapt to the way things are now.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
I mean, you're both right. You CAN clone monopoly. You can even clone its board shape and mechanics down to the T. What you'd have to do is reskin it entirely, however. And Hasbro can still come after you (even if they'd lose the suit) and cost you a shit load of money just because they have lawyers on retainer that are already getting paid. Which is why I assume most or all monopoly-like clones are simply game designers going to Hasbro and pitching a reskin, giving up X% of the profits for licensing, and then making their game with Hasbro's distribution pipeline.

You could technically go and make monopoly though, change the concepts tied to the  mechanics (properties become... I don't know... deific domains? and instead of buying them you're investing spiritual energy, and other deities transgressing into your domain have their energy leeched into you because they're fueling your core ideologies) then you're fine.

But some people seem to think you could just make the same game, switch out words like 'jail' to 'prison' and 'property/deed' to 'land/bill of ownership' and be OK. But that is very much not a safe space. You never know for sure if someone is going to get you in infringement cases, so nothing is ever truly safe nor a guaranteed landmine  (which is why IP law is so stupid. It should be far less nebulous) but I've never understood the desire to risk it and feel like the only reason someone would is if they have never had an original idea in their brain. replies.author: zorecknor
replies.body:
IANAL, but my understanding is that you cannot copyright the code and the assets individually, but you can copyright them as a whole game.

You can generate a character with AI and make a game with it. Your game can be copyrigthed because you need significant human input (if anything on the design of the mechanics), but anybody can use your character anyway they want (except the exact same game) because it cannot be copyrigthed.

replies.author: tipsystatistic
replies.body:
Your understanding is incorrect. You can’t copyright anything the AI created unless you substantially change it. If you have mixed elements, you hand drew a character, only that character can be copyrighted.

Again just Google it or ask your AI and let me know if you find differently.

replies.author: zorecknor
replies.body:
Well, my AI told me more or less what I said:

* Someone who copies your **whole game** would probably infringe my compilation copyright. (By compilation it means me designing systems, deciding which asset goes where, designing maps, planing the development, deciding about code structure, etc, and thus producing the final game).
* Someone who takes **individual AI assets** or **chunks of AI-written code** and uses them elsewhere probably would not infringe. You’d have no copyright in those pieces.
* Your planning and design work protects you against close copies of the overall expression. It doesn’t stop someone from building a similar game with the same mechanics.

So the game  can be copyrighted as a WHOLE, the individual elements/assets will not be protected. Of course you need to provide proof of that significant human expression. If I just prompt "there are assets in this directory. Make a game, make no mistakes" the game definitively will not be copyrightable.

A friendly reminder that the Copyright office doesn't grant copyright. It's purpose is for proof. Human creations are born with copyright, if you don't register it, you still have it, it's just going to be harder to prove it in court, but that doesn't mean impossible.  
  
Second.  The law hasn't solved how and what or when stuff created with LLM are copyrightable or not (Like it happened with Camera and Pictures) , the office is an administrative agency that stablish guidelines, we need to wait for legislators or judges to actually solve the issue. The closest case so far I know is Thaler v. Perlmutter and the "Creator" literally told the office he had 0 creative input. I don't know any case where someone prompted an image and decides how to it looks and then has ended up in court. This is not minor as the court could consider this tweaking creative human input and grant copyright.   
  
Aka: The discussion is freaking open and the doctrine is currently being developed.

But yeah. Writing a prompt once is most likely not protected.

comments.author: KevinDL
comments.body:
I saw this developer's post on r/gamedev claiming their game had been cloned, so I checked both Steam pages. Frankly, I'm struggling to see the issue. There are similarities in the core concept, presentation, and some UI elements, but that's hardly evidence of copying. Developers working in the same genre or design space will naturally arrive at similar solutions. UI layouts in particular often follow established design conventions because they make sense from a usability perspective. Two developers arriving at similar implementations doesn't automatically mean one copied the other.

What bothers me more is turning those similarities into a public accusation without compelling evidence. At that point, it starts to look less like a legitimate intellectual property concern and more like an attempt to generate sympathy at another developer's expense. That's not something I think we should be encouraging.

Competition is a reality of commercial game development. Having a similar concept doesn't give you exclusive ownership of an idea, and another developer bringing a comparable product to market isn't inherently doing anything wrong. Your competitive advantage comes from execution, production quality, differentiation, and how effectively you position and market your game. Focus on building the better product and giving customers a reason to choose it. If a competing game is enough to provoke this kind of reaction, you'll have a hard time navigating the realities of this industry.
